summary: Our gamified software will feature a sleep-monitoring watch connected to a coffee brewing machine in space that will analyze sleep patterns and deliver personalized coffee shots for the astronauts. It addresses the challenge by timing when and how much caffeine intake would prevent physical and mental health challenges that occur from inadequate sleep. Caffeine is important for influencing a human’s circadian system. A controlled caffeine intake may help balance an astronaut’s daily routine and feelings of alertness. The software takes sleep data, analyzes it, adapts coffee shots based on how an individual reacts to caffeine, then gives suggestions on caffeine intake. The game features different visuals of coffee, animating different faces to express how much sleep the astronaut got. The different portions of coffee would be represented by an animation of the coffee cup filling up. It works by receiving input from the watch, seeing the sleep-wake cycles, and the output is the game. The game would give the sleep report and suggestions. The benefits are that the program is fun and easy to see health at a glance with a gamification system, dynamic chart reporting the results, and color coding. We hope to achieve an improved mood and sleep for astronauts. We used a digital screen, coffee machine, and Claude to develop our project.
details:
Orbit Brew is gamified software that attaches to the ISSpresso machine and pairs it with a sleep-monitoring watch. The watch reports how long each astronaut slept and how rested they felt, and the software turns that into a sleep score. A short questionnaire and daily check-ins (crashing, steady, or wired) teach it when each person slumps and when they most want coffee. It then builds a personal plan around their wake and bed times, even on a Mars-length day, and the ISSpresso screen delivers portioned shots at the right moments. Poor sleep adds a little extra, great sleep lightens the shot, and a firm caffeine cutoff protects the next night's rest. A Tamagotchi-style coffee cup and barista make it friendly. The cup sleeps during rest hours, looks groggy, energized, or jittery depending on how the astronaut is doing, and fills with coffee to show the caffeine in the body. Green, amber, red, and blue colors show whether coffee is fine, a last call, off limits, or sleep time.

Astronauts have no natural sunrise or sunset, so their body clocks drift and their sleep suffers, which can weaken attention, memory, and mood. Caffeine influences the circadian system as well as alertness. Taken at the right time it supports a steady rhythm, and taken too late it can delay the body clock and cut sleep short. By timing and sizing each shot to the individual's own sleep data, Orbit Brew helps reduce the physical and mental health risks of inadequate sleep while keeping crews alert during their slumps. The goal is more rested, steadier, and healthier astronauts on long missions, and points, streaks, and badges reward good timing rather than simply more coffee.

The prototype is a web app built with Claude using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with SVG graphics for the cup and day dial. The intended hardware is any sleep-tracking watch plus the ISSpresso machine with the screen mounted as an attachment. In the prototype the watch sync is simulated, so real hardware integration is the next step. The project is creative because it treats coffee as a health tool and turns invisible things, like sleep quality and caffeine in the body, into a face and a fill level anyone can read at a glance. Our team considered safety first, with daily caffeine limits and a bedtime cutoff, along with individual differences, ease of use for tired crews, privacy of sleep data, and medical oversight, since a flight surgeon should review every default number
